goal.title: Prepare for Python interviews by understanding program behavior
goal.focusAreas: Interpret reference sharing and control flow instead of memorizing outputs

objectives: Trace a nested mutable value through aliasing, an outer slice copy and later mutation or rebinding; the final returned structural value must depend on the details.
Trace conditional accumulation and an actual loop exit or loop else; distinguish the paths using the supplied data rather than merely defining break.

sourceDocuments.name: Python assignment and shallow copying
sourceDocuments.text: Assignment binds names to objects. A shallow copy recreates the outer container while preserving references to its members. A whole-list slice is a shallow copy.

sourceDocuments.name: Python loop control
sourceDocuments.text: Loop else runs after normal completion. A break, return or raised exception skips it. Break exits the innermost enclosing loop; continue advances that loop.

artifact.source:
def f(x):
 a=[[1,2],[3,4]]
 b=a[:]
 a[0].append(x)
 a[1]=[5]
 return b

options.reason: The shallow copy shares inner lists, so append modifies b[0]. Rebinding a[1] does not affect b[1], which still holds [3,4].
This assumes rebinding a[1]=[5] also updates b[1], but the slice copy gives b its own reference to the original [3,4] object.
This assumes a[:] made a deep copy, but it only copies the outer list; inner lists remain shared, so append is visible through b[0].
This combines a deep-copy assumption for b[0] with a shared-reference assumption for b[1]—the opposite of what actually happens.

candidates.explanation: a[:] creates a shallow copy: b gets a new outer list but shares the same inner lists. a[0].append(9) mutates the shared inner list, visible via b[0]. a[1]=[5] only rebinds a's slot, leaving b[1] as [3,4].
